laws.rule: The recreational use of marijuana (Cannabis) is subject to local laws and regulations. It's illegal to transport marijuana (Cannabis) across Canada's international borders (including the United States), even if you are entering or leaving the country. If you break the law, you can receive criminal penalties, including jail time. Make sure you know the local cannabis laws about: legal age possession purchase sharing impairment production Local health authorities have reported illegal drugs may be mixed with more potent substances that can lead to health issues including overdose and death.

laws.rule: To drive in Canada, you may need: an International Driving Permit (IDP) and a valid Australian licence Get an IDP before you leave Australia. You can drive for up to one year with an IDP and your Australian licence. After that, you'll need a local driver's licence. Requirements may vary in different provinces and states. For details see Driving in Canada.
laws.heading: Driving permit

laws.rule: Declare currency or monetary instruments (cash, cheques, money orders, bank drafts) worth CAN$10,000 or more, in any mix of currencies, when you enter or leave Canada. Carrying that much is not illegal; not declaring it is. CAN$10,000 is about A$10,160 (RBA 30 Oct 2026: A$1 = CAD 0.9838).
laws.penalty_signal: All of it can be seized; it can be returned after a penalty of 5% to 50% of the seized amount. Not returned if suspected to be proceeds of crime

laws.rule: Visitors must declare all alcohol they bring in. The duty-free limit is 1.5 litres of wine, or 1.14 litres of spirits, or 8.5 litres of beer or ale (or 1.14 litres of wine and spirits combined). Minimum age to bring it in is 18 in Alberta, Manitoba and Quebec and 19 elsewhere. Amounts over the limits may need a provincial or territorial permit as well as duty and tax.
laws.penalty_signal: Duties and taxes payable on declared amounts; undeclared goods can be seized

laws.rule: Visitors must declare tobacco and vaping products. The duty-free limits are 200 cigarettes, 50 cigars, 200 grams of manufactured tobacco, 200 tobacco sticks, and 12 or fewer vaping containers (each up to 120 mL of liquid or 120 g of solid). Minimum age to bring them in is 18 anywhere in Canada. Duties and taxes can apply to any declared amount.
laws.penalty_signal: Duties and taxes payable; undeclared goods can be seized

laws.rule: Declare all food, plant and animal products when you arrive, including any pets. Undeclared items can be seized.
laws.penalty_signal: Penalty of up to CAN$1,300 (about A$1,320) for not declaring

laws.rule: Cannabis is legal inside Canada under its law, but taking it across the border in either direction is a serious criminal offence. Any cannabis or cannabis product with you, in any quantity, must be declared to the Canada Border Services Agency; this includes products made from cannabis or hemp.
laws.penalty_signal: Cannabis can be confiscated, with criminal charges possible; a monetary penalty of up to CAN$2,000 for not declaring

items.text: Psilocybin is a restricted drug (Schedule 4) under Canada's Controlled Substances Regulations (SOR/2025-242), in force from 1 October 2026. They replace the 2022 Special Access Program class exemption: section 6 lets a person possess a Schedule 4 Part 1 restricted drug only if, among other listed cases, they obtained it for their own use from a practitioner named in a Health Canada letter of authorization. Otherwise possession stays illegal; no retail or recreational access.
MDMA is also a Schedule 4 restricted drug under SOR/2025-242 (in force 1 October 2026), with the same narrow letter-of-authorization route as psilocybin.
The recreational use of marijuana (Cannabis) is subject to local laws and regulations.
It's illegal to transport marijuana (Cannabis) across Canada's international borders (including the United States), even if you are entering or leaving the country.

Make sure you know the local cannabis laws about: legal age possession purchase sharing impairment production Local health authorities have reported illegal drugs may be mixed with more potent substances that can lead to health issues including overdose and death.

culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: In national parks: never feed, approach or follow wildlife. Keep at least 30 m from deer, elk, moose and sheep, and 100 m from bears, wolves, coyotes and cougars. Leave rocks, fossils, antlers and plants where they are.
culture-and-protocol.sacred_or_restricted_places: Look at and record Indigenous and other cultural sites, but leave artefacts, bones and remains exactly as found. Removing or defacing cultural artefacts is illegal.
culture-and-protocol.cultural_authority: Parks Canada; the Indigenous Nations whose lands the parks are on.
culture-and-protocol.note: From federal government guidance; there is no single national etiquette page.

drone-pilot-pathway.summary: No public operator directory found. Foreign pilots need a Canadian drone pilot certificate and usually a Foreign SFOC-RPAS; flying for a Canadian RPOC holder avoids the SFOC. Destination Canada offers a b-roll library.

items.text: Not yet checked: no public Transport Canada directory of RPOC holders was found on the pages read.
Pilots of drones of 250 g or more need a Transport Canada drone pilot certificate; special operations need an SFOC-RPAS; operators may hold an RPAS Operator Certificate (RPOC).

Foreign pilots need a Canadian drone pilot certificate even if licensed at home, and usually a Foreign SFOC-RPAS (about 30 working days). Foreign commercial operators qualify only under a free trade agreement that allows the service. Employees or agents of a Canadian RPOC holder don't need a Foreign SFOC, so hiring or flying for a local RPOC holder is the simpler route.
Destination Canada's Canada Media Toolkit includes a b-roll footage library cleared for editorial and non-commercial coverage; the Brand Canada Library has photo and video assets after registration.
